justificativa: The test logs in with the stated admin credentials, calls /api/v1/users/me with the bearer token, and asserts email, is_superuser and is_active. It has no explicit non-empty body check, though a parsed dict with an email field covers it. Endpoints, form login and response fields match the spec.

The test checks a 404 and a 'detail' string, but it authenticates as a newly signed-up regular user, not the required superuser admin@example.com. It also matches only a loose 'not found' substring rather than the exact 'Item not found' value, so a faulty message could pass.

The test follows every requirement step: superuser login, PATCH /users/me/password with current and new passwords, checking 200 and the exact message, login with the new password, revert, and login with the original password. Payloads and endpoints match the spec, and the new password meets the 8-40 length limit.

The test ignores the required superuser scenario: it registers a new user and authenticates as that user, not as admin@example.com. It does assert the 200 status and the updated title, description, id and owner_id. Calls match the spec. A faulty superuser update path would not be caught.

The test performs the required signup, login, and PATCH /users/me with email 'invalid@', then asserts 422. Its extra checks on the error body match the documented HTTPValidationError schema and do not contradict the requirement. The spec documents all endpoints, auth, and status codes used, so a correct implementation should pass and a faulty one should fail.

The test asserts the required 422 for a null password on the signup endpoint, but uses a different email and omits the specified full_name, so it does not set up the exact scenario. The extra check on the password error location is reasonable and consistent with the spec's validation error schema.

The test logs in with the stated superuser credentials, PATCHes /api/v1/users/{uuid} with a random UUID and full_name payload, and asserts both the 404 status and the exact 'detail' message, matching every requirement clause. The endpoint, auth and form-login usage follow the spec; the 404 is undocumented but required by the requirement.

Logs in as the seeded superuser, creates a user with a random email, and checks the required email, id, and is_active fields. The status check is stricter than the 200-299 range, and it adds unrequested checks on full_name and is_superuser, which are reasonable but extra. Endpoints and payloads match the spec.

The test follows every requirement step: login as admin, PATCH /users/me/password with current and new passwords, checks 200 and the exact message, verifies login with the new password, reverts, and verifies login with the original password. The new password (20 chars) fits the 8–40 limit, and the calls match the spec.

The test logs in as the stated superuser, deletes a random UUID item, and asserts the 404 status and the exact 'Item not found' detail, covering every requirement outcome. The spec lists no 404 for DELETE /items/{id}, but the requirement demands it, so that is acceptable and costs only a little consistency.

Sends the 7-character new_password to the documented endpoint and asserts the 422 the requirement demands, plus a new_password validation error. The message check on 'at least 8' goes beyond the requirement and depends on the framework's wording, a small risk on a correct implementation.

The test logs in as the superuser, sends identical current and new passwords to PATCH /api/v1/users/me/password, and checks the 400 status and exact 'detail' message, all required by the requirement. The 400 is undocumented in the spec but the requirement demands it. Asserting token_type presence is a minor extra assumption.

The test registers via /users/signup, logs in with form-encoded credentials, and creates an item with a bearer token. It checks status 200, title and description equality, presence of id, and owner_id equal to the signup user's id. All calls match the spec, and no unstated behaviour is asserted.

The test posts to /api/v1/users/signup with a null email and the stated password and name, then asserts status 422. Extra checks on the HTTPValidationError structure and the email field in loc match the spec's documented schema. The exact content-type string comparison is a minor fragility but should hold for FastAPI.

The test registers a normal user via /users/signup, logs in via /login/access-token, and calls GET /users/{random uuid} with the bearer token. It asserts the 403 status and the exact detail body the requirement specifies. All endpoints, payloads and status codes match the spec.

The test registers a user via signup, logs in with a wrong password using form-encoded data matching the spec, and asserts both the 400 status and the exact detail message the requirement demands. The 400 response isn't documented in the spec, but the requirement mandates it, so that is not penalised.

The test follows the required steps: signup, login, then PATCH /users/me/password with a 129-character new_password, asserting 422. The spec's maxLength of 40 makes 422 the correct outcome. Endpoints, payloads and the signup 200 and login flow match the spec. The cleanup step is harmless.

The test follows every requirement step: signup, login, item creation, self-deletion with the message check, superuser login, and a GET expecting 404 with detail 'Item not found'. Endpoints and payloads match the spec. The 404 relies on the backend cascading item deletion with the user, which is implied but not spec-documented.

The test performs the required signup, login, and oversized-description item creation, then asserts 422 as the requirement demands. Calls match the spec's paths, form-encoded login, and bearer auth. The message check accepts two common validation wording variants, so a correct 422 with different wording could fail it.

The test follows every requirement step: superuser login, /users/me to get the id, DELETE with the same token, then checks 403 and the exact detail message. The 403 is undocumented in the spec but the requirement demands it. The JSON content-type check is a minor extra assumption.

The test generates the three random values, posts them to /users/signup, and asserts 200 plus matching email and full_name. It then logs in with the form-encoded credentials and checks for an access token. The extra test-token check is consistent with the spec, and the password length satisfies the 8 to 40 character constraint.

The test follows every requirement step: admin login, private user creation, retrieval by id with the token, and checks of status 200 plus email and full_name. Endpoints, form-encoded login, bearer auth and response fields all match the spec. Sending an auth header to the unauthenticated private endpoint is harmless.

The test posts the exact scenario (256-char full_name, which exceeds the UserRegister maxLength of 255) and asserts 422. The extra checks on the detail list follow the documented HTTPValidationError/ValidationError schema. A correct implementation should return 422, and one that accepts the value would fail.

The test covers signup, login, and the 403 status on delete. It only checks that 'detail' is non-empty, not that it equals "The user doesn't have enough privileges". It never verifies that the second user still exists by logging in as them. Endpoints and fields match the spec.

The test covers the full change, login, revert, and re-login flow with 200 checks. However, it only asserts 'message' is a string, not that it equals 'Password updated successfully' as the requirement demands. Endpoints, auth, and payloads match the spec.

Asserts the required 404 for a non-existent user, but substitutes a random UUID email for the specified 'jVgQr@example.com'. The 404 is not in the spec's responses, though the requirement demands it. Exact Content-Type equality is slightly brittle but fine for FastAPI JSON responses.

The test logs in as admin and patches a random UUID, but sends an empty payload instead of setting full_name to 'Updated_full_name'. It checks that 'detail' is a string but never asserts the required exact text, so a wrong message would pass. The 404 is undocumented in the spec but the requirement demands it.

The test checks user IDs rather than the emails the requirement asks to verify, and never checks the 'data' and 'count' keys or email matching explicitly. It uses the /private/users endpoint instead of the public create-user API. The hard-coded count==3 assumes a clean seed.

Login, the PATCH to /users/me/password and the 400 status check match the requirement and spec. However, the test only checks that 'detail' is a string and never asserts it equals 'Incorrect password', so a wrong message would still pass.",

Covers login, two user creations, list retrieval, 200 status, 'data' and 'count' structure, and email presence. It checks emails and IDs separately rather than verifying that each listed record pairs the created ID with its email. Endpoints and payloads match the spec.

Sets up the superuser login and same-password PATCH correctly and checks status 400 and a non-empty string 'detail'. It never asserts the required exact message 'New password cannot be the same as the current one', so a wrong message would still pass. The 400 is undocumented in the spec but the requirement demands it.

The test logs in as the seeded superuser, creates a user with a unique email, repeats the identical request, and asserts a 400 status and no '_id' key in the body, covering every requirement assertion. The 400 response is undocumented in the spec but is required by the requirement, so it is not penalised. Cleanup is included.

The test calls the correct PATCH endpoint with the admin token, but accepts 400, 401, 403 or 422 instead of requiring 400, and never checks the detail message 'Incorrect password'. It also adds unrequired login checks. A faulty implementation returning 401 would pass.

The test ignores the required superuser login (admin@example.com / password123). It signs up a fresh regular user and uses that token instead. Item creation and list checks are reasonable, but the superuser authentication and the 'at least two items' check against the superuser's view are not exercised. Endpoints and payloads match the spec.

The test follows the requirement exactly: it signs up a normal user, obtains a bearer token via the password grant, posts to /api/v1/users/ with random email and lowercase password, and asserts 403. Signup and token calls match the spec. The 403 is not documented in the spec, but the requirement demands it, so it is not penalised.

The test logs in as the superuser, creates two users with distinct emails, lists users, and checks the 200 status, the 'data' and 'count' keys, and that both emails appear with matching values. Endpoints, bodies, bearer auth and response fields all match the spec. Hardcoded emails are safe on a fresh seed.

The test follows the required steps: signup, token login, then POST /api/v1/users/ with the normal user's bearer token, and asserts 403. The 403 is not documented in the spec, which the requirement permits. The extra non-empty-body check on non-JSON responses is a minor, unstated assumption.

The test covers the signup status and the email and full_name checks, but it uses hardcoded values instead of generated ones and omits the required login verification. It also asserts is_active and is_superuser values the requirement does not mention. Spec endpoints and fields are used correctly.

The test never registers a new normal user via signup. It retrieves the admin's own record instead, so it checks admin's email and id rather than the created user's. It only checks that is_active exists, not that it is true. Endpoints and auth match the spec.

The test covers login, item creation and a 200 delete, but never checks the exact message 'Item deleted successfully' (it only requires a non-empty string) and omits the required follow-up GET expecting 404. A faulty implementation that doesn't actually delete would still pass. Calls match the spec.

The test follows the required flow: signup, admin login, GET by id, then checks status, email and id. It asserts only that is_active is a boolean, not that it is true, which is a partial check of a stated outcome. Endpoints and payloads match the spec.

Correctly signs up, logs in, and calls POST /api/v1/users/ with a normal token, asserting 403. It uses fixed rather than random email and a mixed-case password instead of a random lowercase string. The extra 'detail' string check is not in the requirement.

The requirement specifies logging in as the seeded superuser (admin@example.com / password123). The test instead signs up a fresh user and uses that account's token, so superuser authentication is never exercised. The 200 and two-items checks are relevant, but a broken superuser login would not be detected. Endpoints and schemas match the spec.

The test accepts 401 as well as 403, so it does not verify the required status. It never checks the 'detail' message equals "The user doesn't have enough privileges". It does verify signup, login and that user2 still exists. Calls match the spec.

Login, token use, and the create-user calls match the spec. However, the test accepts 409 as well as 400, so a non-compliant status would pass. It never checks that the duplicate response lacks an '_id' field, and it asserts a 'detail' key the requirement does not mention.

The test logs in as the seeded superuser, creates a user, repeats the same creation, and asserts a 400 status and no '_id' field, covering every stated assertion. The 400 response is not documented in the spec, but the requirement demands it, so it is not penalised.

Sets up two signed-up users, logs in, and asserts 403, but only checks that 'detail' exists rather than the exact required message. It also targets another existing user's ID, not a random UUID as specified. Signup, login and the 403 path are consistent with the spec's flows, though 403 is undocumented.

Login, random UUID, PATCH /users/{id} and the 404 check match the requirement. However, the exact 'detail' text is never asserted (only a loose non-empty check), and the payload uses different values than the required 'Updated_full_name'. The spec is consistent; 404 is demanded by the requirement.

Covers the full flow and checks login with the new password, but only asserts 'message' is present in the reset response, not the exact required JSON. Token extraction from HTML by regex is a doubtful assumption. Endpoints and payloads match the spec.

The test omits the required superuser login and Authorization header, and uses different token and password values. It checks status 400 and that a string 'detail' exists, but never asserts the exact value 'Invalid token'. The strict Content-Type equality check is doubtful.

The test covers the login part well (status 200, access_token non-empty, token_type bearer), but omits the required GET /api/v1/users/me call and its email check entirely. It would pass even if the protected endpoint were broken. Calls and fields match the spec.

The test checks the 404 status but only that a 'detail' key exists, not that its value is 'Item not found', so a wrong message would pass. It also logs in with 'changethis' instead of the required password123, so it does not follow the stated scenario.

The test calls DELETE /users/{user_id} instead of the required DELETE /users/me, and never checks the 'User deleted successfully' message or the 'Item not found' detail. A non-superuser deleting another user would be rejected, so the 200 assertion would likely fail on a correct implementation.

Asserts the required 422 for a 256-character description, but ignores the specified email 'test55@example.com' and password 'validpass123', using random values instead. Its check for the exact message 'ensure this value has at most 255 characters' is implementation-specific (Pydantic v1 wording) and may fail on a correct implementation.

The test is truncated mid-definition ('def api_base_url' with no body), so it is a syntax error and contains no request or assertion for the 422 signup check. The spec's UserRegister full_name maxLength of 255 makes the requirement consistent, but the test cannot run.

The requirement calls for registering the existing 'admin@example.com' and expects 400 with a specific 'detail' message. The test uses a fresh email and expects 422 with a validation-error list, so it never checks the required outcome. Its 422 expectation for duplicates is not documented in the spec.

Uses test@example.com instead of the required test15@example.com and only checks that the message is truthy, not the exact text 'Password recovery email sent'. Cleanup parses a user ID from the message and calls authenticated endpoints without auth, so it would fail even on a correct implementation.

Signup, recovery call, status code and message checks match the requirement and spec. The mailcatcher check likely fails on a correct service: MailCatcher's /messages recipients are typically formatted as '<email>', which the exact-match comparison does not handle, and headers are not in that listing.

The scenario is set up correctly, but the test asserts 403 instead of the required 400 and never checks the 'Not enough permissions' detail value. It would fail a conforming implementation. It also adds an extra check that the item is unchanged, and the 403 expectation is undocumented in the spec.

The test contains only import statements. It registers no user, logs in, posts an item, or asserts a 422 status, so it cannot verify the requirement. Nothing in it contradicts the spec, but it has no calls to check against it.

The test logs in as testuser/testpassword instead of the required admin@example.com/password123, so login likely fails before any item is created. It also never checks owner_id, which the requirement explicitly demands. Endpoints and payloads otherwise match the spec.

The test is truncated to the single line 'from requests.auth import', which is a syntax error, so it cannot run. It contains no registration, login, retrieval or assertion logic, so none of the required behaviour is checked.

The requirement asks to register with admin@example.com (existing superuser) and expect HTTP 400 with detail 'The user with this email already exists in the system'. The test instead uses a fresh email, registers it first, and expects 422 with a validation-list structure. It contradicts the required status and body, and does not use the seeded superuser email.

Sends the invalid-email signup and asserts the required 422, which is documented in the spec. However, it also asserts pydantic-v1-style msg 'Invalid email' and type 'value_error.email', which the requirement and spec don't guarantee and which likely fail on a correct pydantic v2 implementation. It also uses a different password than the requirement specifies.

The test contains only import statements. It registers no user, attempts no login, and makes no assertions on the 400 status or the 'Incorrect email or password' detail, so it cannot verify the requirement. No calls exist to contradict the spec, but nothing is checked against it either.

The test follows the required steps and asserts 422. However, its error-message check accepts only "Title should not be empty" or pydantic v1's "ensure this value has at least". A pydantic v2 backend, which the spec's schema style suggests, returns "String should have at least 1 character", so a correct implementation would fail.

The test body is empty: it contains only a comment and no login, user creation, or assertions. It cannot verify the required status range, email, id, or is_active fields, so it would pass on any implementation, correct or not. Spec consistency is neutral because no calls are made.

The test contains only imports and no test function, so it performs no login, user creation, listing, or assertions. It cannot pass meaningfully or detect any violation of the requirement. Spec consistency is neutral because no endpoints are called.

Sets up registration, correct-password login and wrong-password login, and checks the user fields, token and 401. It loosens the required 201 login status to 200/201 and uses different credentials, which is incidental. Requests and status codes match the spec, and the test would catch an accepted wrong password.

Uses different username and email than the required 'testuser123' and 'test@example.com', and never asserts the token is non-empty. The cleanup reads user['id'], which the User schema does not define, so a correct implementation would likely raise KeyError and fail.

The test registers both users, creates one article each, and checks the author-filtered results for articlesCount, array length and titles, plus the unfiltered count of 2. Endpoints, auth headers, and response fields match the spec. Relying on a clean seed without other articles is reasonable under the stated environment.

The test registers both users via POST /users, creates one article each, then filters GET /articles by author. It asserts articlesCount is 1, a single returned article with the correct title, and the correct author username for each user. All calls and response fields match the spec, and the assertions follow directly from the requirement.

Creates both users and articles with the required data, then checks articlesCount and the single returned title for each author filter. Also verifies the author username, which fits the stated author-article relationship. Response shapes match the spec, including the unwrapped article from POST and the wrapped user from POST /users.

Covers the full flow: user registration, article creation, PUT, GET, and checks that 'created' is unchanged and 'updated' is strictly newer. Responses match the spec's wrappers. It assumes the slug stays the same after a title change, which the spec does not guarantee, so a correct implementation could fail.

Uses random username/email instead of the required 'jwtuser1' values and never checks the email claim in the JWT payload. It also replaces the required GET /api/user verification with a PUT /user call. It does check id and username claims against the PUT response, which the spec documents. Wrong email claims would pass undetected.

Covers registration/login, 201 creation, title, description, tagList, slug prefix, and GET by slug with 200 and title. It loosens the lowercase requirement by checking slug.lower() instead of the slug itself, so an uppercase slug would pass. Endpoints, auth header, and wrapped/unwrapped responses match the spec.

Checks the PUT status, updated title/description and unchanged slug. It omits the required GET by original slug to verify persisted values, and it uses a random user instead of 'updateuser1'. It also adds unrequired body and timestamp assertions, though these don't contradict the spec.

Covers follow, unfollow, and the profile following=false check, but omits the required self-unfollow 400 assertion, so a faulty implementation could pass. It also uses random usernames and a different password instead of the specified accounts. The extra idempotent-unfollow assertion is not required by the requirement or guaranteed by the spec.

Follow and unfollow calls use the right token, but the profile lookups after follow and unfollow are unauthenticated, so a correct implementation returns following=false and the test fails. It also ignores the specified usernames and never checks the profile with user1's token.

Covers article creation, three comment POSTs, unique integer IDs and body preservation. It does not assert exactly three comments returned (only at least three matches), and it uses a dynamic username and email instead of the specified ones. Endpoints, auth and response fields all match the spec.

The test creates both users and articles, then checks articlesCount, list length and titles for each author filter, matching the requirement. However, the spec documents POST /articles as returning an unwrapped article, but create_article reads response.json()["article"], which would raise KeyError on a spec-conforming server. That makes the test fail on a correct implementation.

Covers the required scenario and checks count, unique ids and bodies. But it expects wrapped 'article' and 'comment' keys from POST create-article and POST comment, which the spec documents as unwrapped or as an article-with-comments object. A spec-conformant server could fail these assertions.

Test uses different users (testuser, another_testuser) than the requirement's feeduser1/feedauthor1/feedauthor2, never checks articlesCount is 0 before following, and never asserts the 'Article By Followed'/'Not Followed' titles. It also passes the fixture function objects (test_user, another_test_user) as payloads, not dicts, so it would fail. Calls /user/delete which is not in the spec.

The test covers every requirement step: registration, article creation, global listing with author check, the DELETE expecting 500, and a post-failure listing check. The DELETE /users/{email} endpoint is absent from the spec, though the requirement demands it, so spec_consistency is only partly penalised. Passing depends on the implementation actually returning 500.

The test creates the user, decodes the payload, and checks username and email, then calls GET /user. It never compares payload id to the user's id, since the User schema has no id field, so that check is missing. It also uses standard base64 on a JWT segment that may be base64url, which could fail on a correct implementation.

Follows the required create/get/delete/get sequence and checks the 200 statuses and empty-object result. However, it reads the created article via an 'article' wrapper, while the spec's UnwrappedArticleResponse has no wrapper. It also asserts the DELETE body equals {}, which the spec (EmptyOkResponse, no content) does not guarantee.

The test is truncated: 'def test_follow_status' has no colon or body, so it is a syntax error and cannot run. It makes no requests and asserts nothing about follow status, so it cannot pass a correct implementation or catch a faulty one.

Covers all three requirement steps: 201 on creation, then 400 with the required message for both duplicate-username and duplicate-email. The 400 status and the message are not documented in the spec (it lists 422), but the requirement demands them. Extra field-type checks are spec-based and reasonable.

The test follows the requirement exactly: registers, logs in, creates a todo, PUTs with mismatched body id, and asserts 400. Spec documents 400 as 'ID mismatch' for PUT and 201 for create, login returns accessToken, so calls are consistent. Minor doubt: register expects 200 which spec documents, fine; the 400 assertion is the only outcome checked, as required.

Registers, logs in, posts a todo with an empty title, and checks for 400 and the 'The Title field is required.' message under the title key. It covers only the empty-title case, not the missing-title case, though the requirement allows either. Calls and fields match the spec.

The test registers two users, logs both in, creates a todo as user1, and has user2 PUT to it, asserting 404. It then fetches as the owner and checks the title and completion are unchanged. It uses different literal titles than the requirement, but the logic matches. Endpoints, payloads and status codes all agree with the spec.

The test registers, logs in, posts a todo with a missing title, and checks the 400 status and the 'The Title field is required.' message in the errors object. It does not cover the empty-string title case the requirement mentions. Endpoints, payloads and the documented 400 response match the spec.

The test registers, logs in, creates a todo, PUTs to /todos/X with a mismatching body id Y=X+1, and asserts 400. Endpoints, bearer auth, and status codes match the spec, which documents 400 for ID mismatch. The optional error-body checks are lenient and cannot cause false failures.

Sets up register, login and POST /todos without title, and checks the 400 status and a title error entry. It never asserts the required message 'The Title field is required.', so a wrong message would still pass. Endpoints, auth and the ValidationProblemDetails shape match the spec.

Sets up two users, creates userA's todo, and asserts userB's GET returns 404, as required. It also checks PUT and DELETE, which go beyond the requirement but match documented 404 behaviour. Endpoints, payloads, auth and status codes are all consistent with the spec.

The test registers and logs in both users, creates a todo as userA, and asserts userB's PUT returns 404. It then checks via GET that the title is still 'UserA Todo'. Endpoints, auth and status codes match the spec. Minor deduction: accepting 400 on registration could mask setup problems.

The test creates the todo with title 'Test Todo' instead of the required 'My Test Todo', so it does not check the specified title. It asserts an exact Content-Type of 'application/json', which may fail on a correct ASP.NET response with a charset suffix. Register, login, create, GET-by-ID and the status and ID checks follow the requirement.

The test registers and logs in two users, creates a todo as user1, and has user2 PUT it, asserting 404. It then fetches as user1 and checks the title is unchanged. Titles differ from the requirement's examples, which is incidental. Endpoints, auth and status codes match the spec.

The test follows every step: registers and logs in both users, creates userA's todo, has userB PUT with a 404 check, then confirms via GET that the title is unchanged. Endpoints, bodies, bearer auth and status codes match the spec. A faulty implementation that returns another status or alters the title would fail.

Registers, logs in, and posts a todo without a title, then checks the 400 status and the exact 'The Title field is required.' message under errors.title. It covers only the missing-title case, not the empty-title case the requirement also names. Endpoints, payloads and the ValidationProblemDetails shape match the spec.
